foods.name: Roti
foods.title: Roti calories: chapati sizes and roti with ghee
foods.description: A medium roti made with 30 g of atta has about {{kcal:medium}} calories. Phulka, chapati and roti with ghee, worked out from IFCT 2017.
foods.answer: One medium roti (about 30 g atta) has about {{kcal:medium}} calories, or about {{kcal:medium_ghee}} with a teaspoon of ghee.
intro: Roti, chapati and phulka are the same flatbread: whole-wheat atta and water, rolled out and cooked on a hot tawa. A phulka is held over an open flame at the end so it puffs. In Gujarat it's rotli, often smaller and thinner than a Punjabi roti.
A plain roti is almost all atta, so its calories follow the size of the dough ball. Ghee or butter on top is what usually raises the number.
foods.portionsCaption: Plain rotis unless stated. Atta weight is before cooking.

recipe.label: Recipe: 100 g atta and about 70 g water, rolled into rotis

ingredients.note: About 70% of the flour weight, as in a published chapati study

recipe.yieldNote: atta x (1 - 0.111) / (1 - 0.33): IFCT's atta is 11.1% water and USDA's cooked chapati is 33% water

portions.label: 1 medium roti with 1 tsp ghee (5 g)

outside.label: Dhaba or restaurant, with ghee
outside.caption: One medium roti. The outside range adds 1 to 2 teaspoons of ghee (5 to 10 g).
outside.basis: No analysed data was found for restaurant or tandoori rotis, so this is a stated assumption: the same roti brushed with 1 to 2 NIN teaspoons (5 ml each) of ghee. Butter has slightly less fat than ghee, so butter rotis sit at or below this range.
text: At home, most rotis reach the plate dry or with a little ghee. At a dhaba or in a restaurant they're often brushed with ghee or butter, and tandoori rotis are usually bigger, which adds more again.
No lab has published a figure for a restaurant roti, so the range below assumes a medium roti with 1 to 2 teaspoons of ghee.

changes: Calories follow the atta, so a roti rolled from a bigger dough ball counts for more, however thin it's rolled.
A teaspoon of ghee or butter on top (5 g) adds about 45 calories, close to half a roti again.
Some kitchens knead the atta with a spoon of oil, which spreads about 45 calories per teaspoon across the whole batch.
These numbers are for whole-wheat atta. Rotis made with maida, or mixed with besan, bajra or jowar, have their own values.
A phulka loses a little water over the flame, so it weighs less, but its calories stay with the atta.
method: The recipe is 100 g of whole-wheat atta with about 70 g of water. Each roti's calories are its share of the atta, using IFCT 2017 values for atta and ghee.
Cooked weight comes from water content: IFCT's atta is about 11% water and USDA's cooked chapati about 33%, so a roti weighs about 1.33 times its atta.

As a check, ICMR-NIN lists one phulka at 80 calories, and 24 g of atta works out here to about {{kcal:phulka}}. The Art & Science of Cooking, a standard Indian cookery textbook, makes four chapatis from 80 g of atta, so each of its chapatis has only 20 g of atta.

faq.q: How many calories are in 1 roti?
faq.a: A medium roti made with about 30 g of atta has about {{kcal:medium}} calories. A phulka is about {{kcal:phulka}}, and a large roti about {{kcal:large}}.

faq.q: How many calories does ghee add to a roti?
faq.a: One teaspoon of ghee (5 g) adds about 45 calories. A medium roti with a teaspoon of ghee comes to about {{kcal:medium_ghee}}.

faq.q: Is a phulka different from a chapati?
faq.a: They're made from the same dough. A [phulka](/calories/phulka/) is puffed over an open flame and is usually smaller, so one phulka counts for less, but gram for gram of atta the calories are the same.

faq.q: How many grams is one roti?
faq.a: A medium roti made with 30 g of atta weighs about {{g:medium}} g once cooked. Sizes vary a lot between kitchens, which is why Slate asks you for your roti size.

faq.q: Which has fewer calories, roti or rice?
faq.a: Per usual serving they're close: 2 medium rotis are about {{kcal:two}} calories, and a 200 ml katori of plain rice is about {{kcal@plain-rice:k200}}. Per 100 g, roti has more, because it holds less water: about {{per100}} against about {{per100@plain-rice}} for cooked rice.

judgement: Medium roti = 30 g atta: NIN's cereal portion is 30 g raw (100 kcal). NIN's phulka at 80 kcal works out to about 24 g of atta. Large = 40 g is a judgement for bigger Punjabi-style rotis.

The textbook chapati (The Art & Science of Cooking via INDB, ASC096) is 80 g atta and 1 tsp ghee for 4 chapatis: 20 g atta each, 72.8 kcal with its share of ghee. INDB's per-100 g value (202 kcal) is not used as a cross-check because INDB doesn't allow for water lost in cooking, so it is per 100 g of dough, not of cooked roti.
Cooked yield 1.33 is derived from water contents (IFCT atta 11.1%, USDA chapati FDC 171844 33%). No Tier 1-3 source weighed a home roti directly.
USDA's commercial chapatis (FDC 171844, 297 kcal per 100 g; FDC 174075, 299 kcal) are not used for values: they are factory-made and contain added fat.
Teaspoon = 5 ml (NIN); 5 g of ghee taken as one teaspoon, matching NIN's 5 g fat portion of 45 kcal.

foods.name: Plain rice
foods.title: Rice calories: per katori, plate and 100 g cooked
foods.description: A 200 ml katori of plain cooked rice has about {{kcal:k200}} calories. White rice by katori, plate and 100 g, worked out from IFCT 2017.
foods.answer: A 200 ml katori of plain cooked white rice (about {{g:k200}} g) has about {{kcal:k200}} calories.
intro: Plain rice here means polished white rice cooked in water until the water is absorbed, with no oil or ghee: the everyday chawal or bhaat that goes with dal.

Rice takes up about three times its raw weight in water, so most of a katori is water. That's why cooked rice has far fewer calories per 100 g than raw rice: about {{per100}} against about {{ing:rice_raw}}.
foods.portionsCaption: Level katoris of plain cooked rice.

recipe.label: Recipe: 100 g raw milled rice, cooked until the water is absorbed
recipe.yieldNote: 2.98 times the raw weight, the measured average for boiled long-grain polished rice (Bognár 2002)
recipe.densityNote: USDA FoodData Central lists 1 cup (236.6 ml) of cooked white rice as 158 g

outside.label: Restaurant, finished with ghee
outside.caption: One 200 ml katori. The outside range adds 0 to 1 teaspoon of ghee (0 to 5 g).
outside.basis: No analysed data was found for restaurant steamed rice. Stated assumption: the same rice with 0 to 1 NIN teaspoon of ghee on top.
text: Steamed rice from a restaurant is usually plain too, so a katori of it counts much the same as yours. Some places finish it with a spoon of ghee or butter, and the bowl is often bigger than a home katori.
We found no lab figure for restaurant rice, so the range below allows for up to a teaspoon of ghee on a 200 ml katori.

changes: Rice boiled in plenty of water and drained ends up wetter, so 100 g of it has fewer calories than rice cooked by absorption. Published values for cooked white rice run from about 105 to 130 calories per 100 g for this reason.
The numbers here are for a level katori. A heaped one holds more.
A teaspoon of ghee or butter on top adds about 45 calories.
Jeera rice, pulao and fried rice are cooked with oil or ghee and have more calories than plain rice.
method: The recipe is 100 g of raw milled white rice (IFCT 2017) cooked until the water is absorbed. Measured yields for boiled white rice are about 2.9 to 3.0 times the raw weight; this page uses 2.98, the average for long-grain polished rice.
For katoris, cooked rice is taken at about 0.67 g per ml, from USDA's 158 g per cup. A plate is the plate in The Art & Science of Cooking, a standard Indian cookery textbook: 100 g of raw rice.

faq.q: How many calories are in 1 katori of rice?
faq.a: A 150 ml katori of plain cooked rice has about {{kcal:k150}} calories, a 200 ml katori about {{kcal:k200}}, and a 250 ml katori about {{kcal:k250}}. These are level katoris.

faq.q: How many calories are in 100 g of cooked rice?
faq.a: About {{kcal:g100}} calories, with about {{protein:g100}} g protein, {{carbs:g100}} g carbs and very little fat.

faq.q: Why do raw and cooked rice have such different calories?
faq.a: Cooking adds water, which has no calories. 100 g of raw rice has about {{ing:rice_raw}} calories and becomes about {{yield}} g of cooked rice, so each 100 g of cooked rice has about a third as much.

faq.q: How many calories are in a plate of rice?
faq.a: A plate made from 100 g of raw rice, about {{g:plate}} g cooked, has about {{kcal:plate}} calories. Plates vary a lot, so a katori is the easier measure.

faq.q: Which has fewer calories, rice or roti?
faq.a: Per usual serving they're close: a 200 ml katori of rice is about {{kcal:k200}} calories and 2 medium rotis are about {{kcal@roti:two}}. Per 100 g, rice has fewer because it holds more water.

foods.name: Dal tadka
foods.title: Dal tadka calories: per katori of toor dal
foods.description: A 200 ml katori of thin dal tadka has about {{kcal:k200}} calories; thick dal has up to about twice that. Toor dal with a ghee tadka, from IFCT 2017.
foods.answer: A 200 ml katori of thin toor dal tadka has about {{kcal:k200}} calories. A thick dal can have close to twice that, because each katori holds more dal.
intro: Dal tadka is toor (arhar) dal cooked soft and finished with a tadka: ghee heated with cumin, garlic, ginger and chilli, poured over at the end. The Gujarati version is thinner, often sweet and sour with jaggery and kokum. Punjabi dal tadka adds an onion and tomato masala and is usually thicker.
Two things decide the number in your katori: how much ghee went into the tadka, and how thick the dal is.
foods.portionsCaption: Thin dal, made as below. A thicker dal has more in each katori.

recipe.label: Recipe: one textbook bowl, 30 g toor dal in 300 ml water with a 10 g ghee tadka

ingredients.note: 5 g cooked into the dal, 5 g in the tadka

recipe.yieldNote: the ingredients added together, with no allowance for water boiled off, as the Indian Nutrient Databank does
recipe.densityNote: thin dal taken as 1 g per ml, like water; a stated assumption

outside.label: Restaurant or dhaba
outside.caption: One 200 ml katori. The outside range is 1.5 to 2 times as thick, with the same ghee per gram of dal.
outside.basis: Published restaurant-style recipes use about the same fat per gram of dal as this textbook dal: Swasthi's dal tadka 2 tbsp ghee plus 1.5 to 2 tbsp oil for 200 g dal (0.24 to 0.27 g per g), against 10 g ghee for 30 g dal here (0.33 g per g). The difference per katori comes mostly from a thicker dal, so the range is 1.5 to 2 times the dal per katori. This is a stated assumption.
text: Restaurant and dhaba dal is usually thicker than everyday home dal, and it's often finished with a second spoon of ghee or butter at the table. Dal fry is cooked with its masala in ghee and tends to be richer again.
Published restaurant-style recipes use about as much ghee per gram of dal as this one, so the range below treats the difference as thickness: the same dal, 1.5 to 2 times as thick.

changes: Most of a thin dal is water. A katori of thick dal can hold twice as much dal, and twice the calories.
Each teaspoon of ghee or oil in the tadka adds about 45 calories to the pot. A generous tadka is the biggest difference between one kitchen's dal and the next.
Gujarati dal often has a spoon or two of jaggery, which adds about 20 calories a teaspoon to the pot.
Onion, tomato and spices add a few calories a katori.
Toor, moong and masoor dal are within a few percent of each other per gram in IFCT 2017, so switching dal matters less than the ghee.
method: The recipe follows the tempered arhar dal in Basic Food Preparation, a standard Indian cookery manual (via the Indian Nutrient Databank), without its spinach: 30 g of toor dal cooked in 300 ml of water, with 10 g of ghee, ginger, garlic, green chilli and cumin. Values are from IFCT 2017.
The cooked weight is the ingredients added together, with nothing allowed for water boiled off, so this is a thin dal. Katoris are worked out at 1 g per ml.

range.text: ICMR-NIN counts half a cup (100 ml) of plain dal at 100 calories, close to twice this page's {{kcal:half}} for the same volume. The difference is thickness: NIN's dal holds far more dal in each cup. Depending on how thick it is, a 200 ml katori of dal tadka can be anywhere from about {{kcal:k200}} to about twice that.
range.reason: NIN's plain dal (100 kcal per 100 ml) is much thicker than the textbook dal (about 57 kcal per 100 ml). Shown as a range on the page.

faq.q: How many calories are in 1 katori of dal?
faq.a: A 200 ml katori of thin dal tadka has about {{kcal:k200}} calories. A thick dal can be close to double, because the katori holds more dal and less water.

faq.q: How much protein is in a katori of dal?
faq.a: A 200 ml katori of this thin dal has about {{protein:k200}} g of protein. A thicker dal has more, in line with the extra dal.

faq.q: How many calories does a ghee tadka add?
faq.a: About 45 calories for each teaspoon of ghee, spread across everyone who eats from the pot. In this recipe the 10 g of ghee adds about 90 calories to a bowl.

faq.q: Which has more calories, dal fry or dal tadka?
faq.a: Usually dal fry, because the dal is cooked into an onion and tomato masala in ghee and is thicker. The dal is the same; the fat and the thickness are what change.

foods.name: Rajma
foods.title: Rajma calories: per katori and per bowl
foods.description: A 200 ml katori of rajma curry has about {{kcal:k200}} calories and {{protein:k200}} g protein. Home rajma, worked out from IFCT 2017.
foods.answer: A 200 ml katori of home rajma curry has about {{kcal:k200}} calories and about {{protein:k200}} g of protein.
intro: Rajma is red kidney beans, soaked overnight, pressure-cooked and simmered in an onion and tomato masala. It's the everyday Punjabi and Jammu dish behind rajma chawal, and Jammu's Bhaderwah rajma has its own GI tag.
The beans carry the protein and most of the calories. The rest comes from oil in the masala, and from cream or a ghee tadka in dhaba versions.
foods.portionsCaption: Home rajma made as below.

recipe.label: Recipe: one textbook bowl, 30 g dry rajma with tomato, onion and 1.5 tsp oil

ingredients.note: Taken up by the beans in soaking and cooking

recipe.yieldNote: cooked beans at USDA's yield for boiled kidney beans (2.62 times the dry weight), plus the other ingredients
recipe.densityNote: rajma curry taken as 1 g per ml; a stated assumption

outside.label: Dhaba or restaurant
outside.caption: One 200 ml katori. The outside range adds a ghee tadka (5 g) and up to 15 g of cream.
outside.basis: From published recipe proportions (Swasthi, Rajma masala): a dhaba-style tadka of 1.5 tbsp ghee for 4 servings (about 5 g each), and a creamy restaurant version with a quarter cup of cream for 4 servings (about 15 g each). Proportions only, not a measured value.
text: Dhaba rajma often gets a second tadka of ghee, and restaurant rajma is sometimes finished with cream or malai, so the difference is the extra fat.
The range below adds about a teaspoon of ghee and up to a tablespoon of cream to a 200 ml katori, in line with published recipe proportions.

changes: The masala here takes about a teaspoon and a half of oil per serving. Each extra teaspoon of oil or ghee adds about 40 to 45 calories.
A tablespoon of cream or malai adds about 30 calories.
A thick, reduced rajma holds more beans in each katori than a thinner one with more gravy.
Rajma chawal is two dishes, so count the rice separately. A 200 ml katori of plain rice is about {{kcal@plain-rice:k200}} calories.
method: The recipe is the rajma curry from The Art & Science of Cooking, a standard Indian cookery textbook (via the Indian Nutrient Databank): 30 g of dry red rajma, 50 g tomato, 25 g onion, ginger, garlic and 1.5 teaspoons of oil for one bowl. Values are from IFCT 2017.
Cooked beans are taken at 2.62 times their dry weight, the ratio between USDA's raw and boiled kidney beans. Katoris are worked out at 1 g per ml.

faq.q: How many calories are in 1 katori of rajma?
faq.a: A 200 ml katori of home rajma curry has about {{kcal:k200}} calories, and a 150 ml katori about {{kcal:k150}}.

faq.q: How much protein is in rajma?
faq.a: A 200 ml katori has about {{protein:k200}} g of protein. Most of it comes from the beans.

faq.q: How many calories are in rajma chawal?
faq.a: Add the two: a 200 ml katori of rajma is about {{kcal:k200}} calories and a 200 ml katori of plain rice about {{kcal@plain-rice:k200}}, so about {{kcal:k200}} plus {{kcal@plain-rice:k200}} for the pair.

faq.q: Why is rajma soaked overnight?
faq.a: Soaking softens the beans so they cook evenly. The beans take up water, which has no calories, so the total doesn't change.

foods.name: Poha
foods.title: Poha calories: per bowl and per plate
foods.description: A plate of poha made with 40 g of dry poha has about {{kcal:plate}} calories. Kanda and batata poha with peanuts, from IFCT 2017 and a textbook recipe.
foods.answer: A plate of poha made with 40 g of dry poha, with potato and peanuts, has about {{kcal:plate}} calories.
intro: Poha is flattened rice, rinsed and tossed in a little oil with mustard seeds, turmeric, curry leaves and green chilli. Maharashtra's kanda poha has onion; Gujarat's bateta poha has potato and usually a little sugar and lemon. Indori poha is steamed and topped with sev and jeeravan.
Plate sizes vary more than recipes, so this page counts poha by the dry poha that went in.
foods.portionsCaption: Poha with potato and peanuts, made as below. Dry poha weight is before rinsing.

recipe.label: Recipe: 40 g dry poha with 30 g potato, 10 g peanuts and 10 g oil
recipe.yieldNote: no published cooked weight for poha, so portions are counted by dry poha

portions.label: 1 very large plate (100 g dry poha)

outside.label: Stall or restaurant
outside.caption: One plate made with 40 g dry poha. The outside range is 1 to 1.5 times the plate with up to a teaspoon more oil. Sev on top isn't counted.
outside.basis: No analysed data was found for stall or restaurant poha. Stated assumption: 1 to 1.5 times the textbook plate with up to 1 tsp (4.5 g) more oil.
text: Poha from a stall or a station is usually a bigger plate, and it's often finished with sev, boondi or extra peanuts. In Indore it comes with jalebi on the side.
We found no lab measurement of stall poha, so the range below assumes a plate up to half as big again with a little more oil. Sev is fried, so a spoon of it on top adds more.

changes: Dry poha is the main ingredient, so a plate made with twice the poha has close to twice the calories.
Each teaspoon of oil adds about 40 calories. This recipe uses 10 g for two bowls.
10 g of peanuts adds about 50 calories.
Sev, boondi and namkeen are fried and add calories quickly, while coriander, lemon and pomegranate add almost none.
Batata poha has a little more than kanda poha because of the potato, but the difference is small.
method: The recipe is the poha in Basic Food Preparation, a standard Indian cookery manual (via the Indian Nutrient Databank): 40 g of rice flakes, 30 g potato, 10 g peanuts, 10 g oil and mustard seeds, for two bowls. Values are from IFCT 2017.

Portions are counted by dry poha, because no reliable cooked weight for poha was found. ICMR-NIN counts a 200 ml cup of poha at about 270 calories, which fits a plate made with a little more poha than the textbook's 40 g.

faq.q: How many calories are in 1 plate of poha?
faq.a: A plate made with 40 g of dry poha, with potato and peanuts, has about {{kcal:plate}} calories. A large plate with 60 g of poha is about {{kcal:large}}.

faq.q: How much protein is in poha?
faq.a: A plate made with 40 g of dry poha has about {{protein:plate}} g of protein, some of it from the peanuts.

faq.q: Does Indori poha have more calories?
faq.a: Usually, because of the sev on top. The poha itself is similar; the fried topping is what adds up.

faq.q: Which has fewer calories, poha or idli?
faq.a: Per plate, idli is usually lower because it's steamed: 2 medium idlis are about {{kcal@idli:two}} calories, against about {{kcal:plate}} for a plate of poha. Toppings and chutney change both.

intro: Idli is a steamed cake of fermented rice and urad dal batter, usually three or four parts rice to one part dal. There's no oil in the batter, so an idli's calories come almost entirely from the rice and dal in it.
Sizes vary a lot, from small home idlis to the large ones in many restaurants. Kanchipuram idli is a different dish: it's made with ghee, sesame oil and pepper, so these numbers don't apply to it.

foods.answer: A home aloo samosa has about {{kcal:one}} calories. A street samosa is usually {{outLo}} to {{outHi}}, depending on its size and how much oil it took up.
intro: A samosa is a maida pastry, kneaded with ghee or oil, filled with spiced potato and peas, and deep-fried. Punjabi samosas are large with a thick, ajwain-spiced crust; Bengal's singara is smaller.
Most of a samosa's calories come from oil: some in the dough, and more taken up in the kadhai. The potato and pea filling adds comparatively little.
foods.portionsCaption: Home aloo samosas made as below, without chutney.

Size factor = vendor weight against this page's samosa; fat factor chosen so total fat matches the measured fat.
text: A peer-reviewed study weighed and tested street samosas from vendors in Delhi and a nearby village. They held about 29 g of fat per 100 g, against about 18 g in a fresh home samosa. Oil that's used again and again, and a thicker crust, are common reasons.
The range below uses those measured samosas: a small one of about 47 g and a large one of about 79 g.

changes: Oil taken up in frying is the biggest single part of a samosa's calories. Frying at the right heat and draining well keeps it lower.
More ghee or oil in the dough makes a flakier crust and adds about 45 calories per teaspoon to the batch.
A large Punjabi samosa can be half as big again as a small one.
ICMR-NIN counts a tablespoon of tamarind chutney with jaggery at about 60 calories. Samosa chaat with curd, chole and sev is a meal of its own.
method: The recipe is the potato samosa in The Art & Science of Cooking, a standard Indian cookery textbook (via the Indian Nutrient Databank): 60 g maida with 2 teaspoons of ghee, 150 g potato, 75 g peas and 12 g of oil for the filling, making 6 samosas. Values are from IFCT 2017.

Frying oil is harder to count. The databank counts all of it as eaten, which gives far too high a number. This page assumes a fresh home samosa ends up about 18% fat, in line with lab-fried samosas (18.3%) and USDA's samosa recipe (17.5%). That works out to about 8 g of oil taken up per samosa.

range.text: ICMR-NIN counts one samosa at 200 calories, a little above this page's {{kcal:one}}. Street samosas are measured as fattier, so a samosa can reasonably be anywhere from about {{kcal:one}} to {{outHi}} calories.
range.reason: NIN's 200 kcal per samosa is about 19% above this page's home samosa; street samosas measured by Gupta et al. hold more fat. Shown as a range.

faq.q: How many calories are in 1 samosa?
faq.a: A home aloo samosa has about {{kcal:one}} calories. A street samosa is usually {{outLo}} to {{outHi}}, depending on its size and the oil.

faq.q: How much fat is in a samosa?
faq.a: A home samosa has about {{fat:one}} g of fat. Street samosas measured in a Delhi study had about 14 to 23 g each.

faq.q: Do baked or air-fried samosas have fewer calories?
faq.a: Yes, because they don't take up frying oil. The crust and filling stay the same, so the difference is roughly the oil, about 8 g in a home samosa here, or about 70 calories.

faq.q: How many calories are in samosa with chutney?
faq.a: Add the chutney: ICMR-NIN counts a tablespoon of tamarind chutney with jaggery at about 60 calories, and a tablespoon of green chutney at very little.

intro: Paneer butter masala, or paneer makhani, is paneer in a tomato gravy finished with butter and a little cream. Some cooks add onion, cashew and a pinch of sugar. Shahi paneer is its paler cousin, richer in cashew and cream and lighter on tomato.
Paneer has about 258 calories per 100 g, so it's most of the dish. The butter and cream decide how much higher it goes.

Each extra tablespoon of butter adds about 100 calories to the pot.
A tablespoon of cream adds about 30 calories, and 10 g of cashew about 60.
Restaurant servings are often two or three times a home katori.

Paneer, vegetables and spices are from IFCT 2017; butter, cream and sugar, which IFCT doesn't list, are from USDA FoodData Central.
The cooked weight is the ingredients added together, as the databank does. Katoris are worked out at 1 g per ml.

faq.q: Which has more calories, paneer butter masala or shahi paneer?

intro: Masala chai is tea leaves boiled with water, milk and sugar, with ginger, cardamom and other spices. In Gujarat it's usually sweet and milky; Mumbai's cutting chai is strong and served as half a glass.

A cutting chai is half a cup, and a large mug can be twice one.
Several cups a day add up: each cup with 2 teaspoons of sugar is about {{kcal:cup2}} calories.

intro: A phulka is a thin whole-wheat roti, cooked briefly on the tawa and then held over an open flame until it puffs. There's no oil in the dough or on the tawa. It's the everyday bread in many Gujarati homes, where it's called rotli, and in Telugu homes, where it's pulka.
Because phulkas are small, most people count them by how many are on the plate. Each one is almost all atta, so the count and any ghee spread on top decide the total.

text: Phulkas from a thali restaurant or a tiffin service are usually about the size of home ones, but they often arrive brushed with ghee, even when you didn't ask for it.
No lab has measured a restaurant phulka, so the range below adds half to one teaspoon of ghee to the same phulka.

changes: The atta in each phulka sets its number. A small one made from 20 g of atta has about {{kcal:small}} calories; one made from 30 g, the size of a medium roti, about {{kcal@roti:medium}}.
Half a teaspoon of ghee adds about 20 calories, and a full teaspoon about 45.
The dry atta used for dusting sticks to the phulka and adds a little, far less than ghee.
Puffing over the flame drives off water. The calories stay the same.
Bajra, jowar or multigrain atta shifts the number a little. Per 100 g, IFCT 2017 puts bajra at {{ing:bajra}} calories and jowar at {{ing:jowar}}, against {{ing:atta}} for wheat atta.
method: The recipe is the chapati in The Art & Science of Cooking, a standard Indian cookery textbook (via the Indian Nutrient Databank): 80 g of whole-wheat atta kneaded with 4 tablespoons of water. The textbook makes four chapatis from it, the small phulka in the table. Its teaspoon of ghee is counted separately here, per phulka, because many homes skip it.
Values for atta and ghee are from IFCT 2017. Cooked weight comes from water content: IFCT's atta is about 11% water and USDA's cooked chapati about 33%, so a phulka weighs about 1.33 times its atta.

faq.q: How many calories are in 2 phulkas?
faq.a: Two phulkas made with about 24 g of atta each have about {{kcal:two}} calories. Three have about {{kcal:three}}, and four about {{kcal:four}}.

faq.q: How many calories are in a phulka with ghee?
faq.a: About {{kcal:one_half_ghee}} with half a teaspoon of ghee, and about {{kcal:one_ghee}} with a full teaspoon. A plain phulka is about {{kcal:one}}.

faq.q: Are phulka and roti the same?
faq.a: They're the same dough. A phulka is usually smaller, is puffed over an open flame and is made without oil, so one phulka counts for less than a medium [roti](/calories/roti/) at about {{kcal@roti:medium}} calories.

faq.q: How much protein is in a phulka?
faq.a: About {{protein:one}} g in a phulka made from 24 g of atta, so 3 phulkas give about {{protein:three}} g. Dal or curd on the side adds more.

faq.q: How many calories are in 100 g of phulka?
faq.a: About {{per100}} calories per 100 g of cooked phulka. That's more than rice per 100 g, because a phulka holds much less water.

The atta is the same as in a roti, so the fat is what sets a paratha apart. In this textbook recipe, the oil is close to half of each paratha's calories.

Parathas vary in size more than rotis. USDA's paratha weighs about 70 g cooked; this one about {{g:one}} g.
Kerala parotta is made with maida and more fat, and stuffed parathas carry their filling, so both have their own values. See [aloo paratha](/calories/aloo-paratha/).
method: The recipe is the plain paratha in The Art & Science of Cooking, a standard Indian cookery textbook (via the Indian Nutrient Databank): 80 g of whole-wheat atta and 2 tablespoons of oil, making 3 parathas. faq.q: How many calories are in a paratha without oil?

faq.q: How much protein is in a paratha?
faq.a: About {{protein:one}} g in one plain paratha. The rest is mostly carbohydrate and fat: about {{carbs:one}} g and {{fat:one}} g.

intro: Aloo paratha is whole-wheat dough stuffed with spiced mashed potato, rolled out and cooked on the tawa with oil or ghee. It's a Punjabi breakfast staple, usually eaten with curd, pickle and a cube of white butter, and it's common in tiffins across north India.
The potato adds less than people expect: in this recipe it's about a tenth of the calories. The atta and the oil on the tawa make up nearly all the rest.

text: At a dhaba, an aloo paratha is often larger, cooked in more ghee or oil and served with a cube of butter melting on top. Amritsari and Murthal-style parathas are known for it.
No lab figure exists for a dhaba aloo paratha, so the range below assumes one up to 1.4 times this size, with up to half as much oil again and 1 to 2 teaspoons of butter.

A teaspoon of butter on top adds about 35 calories, and a tablespoon about 100.
A thicker filling adds less than you'd think: 50 g more potato is about 35 calories.
A katori of curd on the side (100 g) adds about 60 calories, and pickle in oil adds more.
Gobi, mooli and methi parathas use lighter fillings than potato. Paneer parathas have more.
method: The recipe is the potato paratha in The Art & Science of Cooking, a standard Indian cookery textbook (via the Indian Nutrient Databank): 80 g of atta, 80 g of potato, 25 g of onion, green chilli and coriander, with 2 tablespoons of oil for 3 parathas. Spices under 1 g each are left out; together they add under 3 calories a paratha. Values are from IFCT 2017.
All the oil is counted as eaten. Curd values are from USDA, because IFCT 2017 has no curd.

faq.q: How many calories are in 1 aloo paratha?
faq.a: A homemade aloo paratha made with about 27 g of atta and 2 teaspoons of oil has about {{kcal:one}} calories. Two have about {{kcal:two}}.

faq.q: How many calories are in aloo paratha with butter?
faq.a: About {{kcal:one_butter}} with a teaspoon of butter, and about {{kcal:one_butter_tbsp}} with a tablespoon. At a dhaba it can be more, because the paratha is often bigger too.

faq.q: How much protein is in an aloo paratha?
faq.a: About {{protein:one}} g. With a 100 g katori of curd it's about {{protein:one_curd}} g.

faq.q: How many calories are in aloo paratha with curd?
faq.a: One aloo paratha with 100 g of curd comes to about {{kcal:one_curd}} calories.

faq.q: Which has more calories, aloo paratha or plain paratha?
faq.a: The aloo paratha, by a little. Made from the same atta and oil, it's about {{kcal:one}} calories against about {{kcal@plain-paratha:one}} for a [plain paratha](/calories/plain-paratha/), because of the potato and onion.

intro: Thepla is a Gujarati flatbread made from whole-wheat atta, often mixed with besan, bajra or jowar, with fresh methi leaves, curd and spices kneaded into the dough. It's rolled thin and cooked on the tawa with a little oil. Because it keeps for days, it's the standard food for train journeys and tiffins, eaten with chhundo, pickle or curd.
A thepla is thinner and smaller than most parathas. The oil in the dough and on the tawa is a little over a third of its calories.

text: Theplas from a farsan shop, a station stall or a packet are close to home ones in size. They're often softer and a little oilier, because extra oil helps them stay soft for days.
We found no lab measurement of shop theplas, so the range below assumes the same size up to 1.2 times bigger, with up to half as much oil again.

changes: The oil on the tawa matters most. Each extra teaspoon spread across a batch adds about 40 calories.
Thinner, smaller theplas count for less each. Rolling the same dough into 14 instead of 11 makes each one about a fifth lighter.
Bajra and besan add a little fat and protein compared with atta alone. Per 100 g, IFCT 2017 puts bajra at {{ing:bajra}} calories and besan at {{ing:besan}}, against {{ing:atta}} for atta.
Chhundo and other sweet pickles are mostly sugar, and oil pickles add fat, so a spoonful on the side counts too.
Dudhi (lauki) thepla and plain masala thepla have less methi and similar flour, so they come out about the same.
method: The recipe is the methi thepla in the Indian Nutrient Databank's open recipe set: 120 g atta, 40 g each of bajra, jowar and besan, a cup of methi leaves, curd and spices, with 1 tablespoon of oil in the dough and 3 for the tawa, making 11 theplas. Values are from IFCT 2017, with curd and chilli powder from USDA.
All the oil is counted as eaten. The 11 theplas follow the databank's serving count, about 25 g of flour each.

faq.q: How many calories are in 1 thepla?
faq.a: About {{kcal:one}} calories for a methi thepla made with about 25 g of flour and its share of the oil.

faq.q: How many calories are in 3 theplas?
faq.a: About {{kcal:three}}. Two are about {{kcal:two}}, and four about {{kcal:four}}.

faq.q: How much protein is in a thepla?
faq.a: About {{protein:one}} g. Besan and curd in the dough add a little more than a plain roti has for the same flour.

faq.q: Is thepla the same as paratha?
faq.a: Both are cooked on the tawa with oil, but a thepla has methi, curd and spices in the dough and is rolled thin without layers. One thepla here is about {{kcal:one}} calories, against about {{kcal@plain-paratha:one}} for a [plain paratha](/calories/plain-paratha/).

foods.answer: One home puri (about 13 g atta, deep-fried) has about {{kcal:one}} calories. Four puris have about {{kcal:four}}, and a large 36 g puri about {{kcal:large}}.
intro: Puri is a small round of whole-wheat dough, deep-fried until it puffs. It's eaten with aloo sabzi as puri bhaji, with chole, or with shrikhand and aamras on festival days. Bengali luchi is the same idea made with maida.
Atta is about half of a puri's calories. Most of the other half is oil the dough takes up in the kadhai, so this page counts that oil from lab data.

outside.caption: One puri. The outside range is up to 1.45 times the size, with up to about a fifth more oil.
outside.basis: Size up to USDA's 36 g puri (FNDDS 51300180) against about 25 g here, so 1.45. Fat up to 1.22 times: Jain et al. 2024 found total fat in Indian fried foods (including puri) rose from a mean of 22.5% to 27.4% of dry weight between the 1st and 32nd frying cycle in the same oil.
text: Puris from a halwai or a puri-bhaji stall are often larger than home ones, and they're fried in oil that's been used many times, which raises the fat a puri takes up.

A lab study of Indian fried foods, puri among them, found total fat rose by about a fifth between the first and the 32nd frying in the same oil. The range below uses that, and a puri up to the 36 g of USDA's puri.

changes: Size matters most. A puri rolled from 20 g of atta has half as much again as one from 13 g.
Oil that's been used many times leaves more fat in each puri: about a fifth more after 32 fryings, in one lab study.
Ghee or oil kneaded into the dough adds about 45 calories per teaspoon across the batch.
Masala puri, palak puri and Bengali luchi are close per gram. Kachori and bhatura have their own values: see [bhatura](/calories/bhatura/).
method: The recipe is the poori in The Art & Science of Cooking, a standard Indian cookery textbook (via the Indian Nutrient Databank): 80 g of whole-wheat atta with a teaspoon of melted fat, making 5 to 6 puris. This page uses 6. Values are from IFCT 2017.

Frying oil is harder to count. The databank counts all of it as eaten, which gives far too high a number. This page assumes a puri ends up with the fat content of USDA's puri, 24.9%, which works out to about 5 g of oil taken up per puri.

range.text: ICMR-NIN counts one puri at 80 calories, a little under this page's {{kcal:one}}. Puris differ in size and in how much oil they take up, so a home puri usually comes to between about 80 and {{kcal:one}}.
range.reason: NIN's 80 kcal per puri is 16% below this page's home puri. The difference is puri size and the oil-uptake assumption. Shown as a range.

faq.q: How many calories are in 1 puri?
faq.a: A home puri made with about 13 g of atta has about {{kcal:one}} calories once fried. A large one, about 36 g, has about {{kcal:large}}.

faq.q: How many calories are in 4 puris?
faq.a: About {{kcal:four}} for four home puris, before the sabzi. Three are about {{kcal:three}}.

faq.q: Which has more calories, puri or roti?
faq.a: A puri has more for its size, because it takes up oil in frying. One small puri is about {{kcal:one}} calories; a medium [roti](/calories/roti/) with more than twice the atta is about {{kcal@roti:medium}}.

faq.q: How much oil does a puri absorb?
faq.a: About 5 g, a little over a teaspoon, for a home puri fried in fresh oil, going by USDA's measured puri at about a quarter fat. Older oil and lower heat leave more.

faq.q: Puri or bhatura, which has more calories?
faq.a: A [bhatura](/calories/bhatura/) is bigger and made with maida, so one bhatura is about {{kcal@bhatura:one}} calories against about {{kcal:one}} for a puri.

intro: Bhatura is a leavened maida bread, kneaded with curd and sometimes a little baking powder, then deep-fried until it puffs into a large round. It's almost always eaten as chole bhature, a Punjabi dish found from Delhi's street stalls to restaurant breakfasts.
A bhatura takes up a lot of oil in frying. In this page's numbers, oil is close to half its calories, and the maida most of the rest.

Size factor = vendor weight against about 51.7 g here; fat factor chosen so total fat matches the measured fat.
text: A peer-reviewed study bought bhaturas from street vendors in Delhi and a nearby village and tested them in a lab. The Delhi bhatura weighed 52 g with 10.2 g of fat, much like the home bhatura here. The village one was smaller, 33 g, and held much less fat.
Restaurant bhaturas for chole bhature can be bigger than either. We found no measurement of those, so the range below covers the two street bhaturas only.

Oil uptake depends on the heat and the oil. A bhatura fried in cooler or much-used oil soaks up more.
Curd and a pinch of sugar in the dough add very little, about 5 calories a bhatura.
A 200 ml katori of chole is a separate dish, and a fried green chilli and onion on the side add a little more.
method: The recipe is the bhatura in The Art & Science of Cooking, a standard Indian cookery textbook (via the Indian Nutrient Databank): 80 g of maida and 20 g of curd with a pinch of sugar, making 2 to 3 bhaturas. This page uses 3. Values are from IFCT 2017, with curd and sugar from USDA.

The databank counts all the frying oil as eaten, which is far too high. No lab has measured a home bhatura, so this page takes the fat content of the bhatura measured from a Delhi vendor, 19.6%, as typical. That's about 10 g of oil taken up per bhatura.

faq.q: How many calories are in 1 bhatura?
faq.a: About {{kcal:one}} for a bhatura made with about 27 g of maida and fried in fresh oil. Half a bhatura is about {{kcal:half}}.

faq.q: How many calories are in 2 bhature?
faq.a: About {{kcal:two}} for two, before the chole.

faq.q: Is bhatura made of maida?
faq.a: Usually, yes. The textbook bhatura is maida with curd. Some homes mix in atta or semolina, which changes the number a little.

faq.q: How much fat is in a bhatura?
faq.a: About {{fat:one}} g in this home bhatura. Street bhaturas tested in a lab held between 3.3 g and 10.2 g, depending on size and the oil.

judgement: Home oil uptake set so fat is 19.6% of the raw dough plus oil, from Gupta et al. 2016's urban bhatura (10.20 g fat in 52.04 g). (1.26 + x) / (126 + x) = 0.196 gives x = 29 g for 3 bhaturas. Moisture lost in frying is not counted.
The resulting bhatura (about 51.7 g raw dough plus oil) is close to the 52 g Delhi bhatura, so 3 bhaturas from 80 g maida fits.
Water in the dough (25 g) is an assumption; it has no calories and only affects weight.
No second analysed source for bhatura energy was found (IFCT, NIN Annexure 8, USDA FNDDS, Europe PMC). INDB counts 480 ml of frying oil (793 kcal per 100 g), so its values aren't used.

foods.answer: A home naan (about 40 g maida) has about {{kcal:one}} calories. A large 10-inch restaurant naan, about 177 g, has about {{kcal:large}}.
intro: Naan is a soft, leavened maida bread, made with curd and milk and baked against the wall of a tandoor. At home it's usually cooked on a tawa and finished over the flame. It's the standard bread with dal makhani, paneer and chicken curries in north Indian restaurants.
Gram for gram, naan has a little more than roti, from the maida, milk and sugar. A restaurant naan has far more mostly because it's so much bigger.

text: A tandoor naan from a restaurant is usually far bigger than one made at home. USDA's survey data puts a 10-inch naan at 177 g, about three times this home naan. Most are brushed with butter too, which is on the [butter naan](/calories/butter-naan/) page.
The range below is for a plain restaurant naan 2 to 3 times the size of the home one.

changes: Size is the biggest variable by far. Half a large restaurant naan has more than a whole home naan.
Butter or ghee brushed on top adds about 35 to 45 calories a teaspoon.
Garlic naan adds butter as well as garlic, and stuffed naans and kulchas carry their filling.
Whole-wheat naan is close per gram: USDA lists it at 286 calories per 100 g, against 291 for plain naan.
method: The recipe is the naan in The Art & Science of Cooking, a standard Indian cookery textbook (via the Indian Nutrient Databank): 80 g of maida with curd, milk, a teaspoon of sugar and half a teaspoon of melted fat, making 2 to 3 naans. This page uses 2. The textbook's teaspoon of butter for brushing is left out here and counted on the butter naan page. Seeds and spices under 1 g are left out.
Values are from IFCT 2017, with curd and sugar from USDA. Cooked weight comes from water content: the dough's solids at the 29.2% water of USDA's naan.

faq.q: How many calories are in 1 naan?
faq.a: A home naan made with about 40 g of maida has about {{kcal:one}} calories. A large restaurant naan is about {{kcal:large}}, because it's about three times the size.

faq.q: Which has more calories, naan or roti?
faq.a: A naan, mainly because it's bigger. Per 100 g naan has somewhat more too: about {{per100}} calories, against about {{per100@roti}} for [roti](/calories/roti/).

faq.q: Is naan made of maida?
faq.a: Usually, yes. Restaurant naan is almost always maida. Whole-wheat naan exists and has about the same calories per gram.

faq.q: How much protein is in a naan?
faq.a: About {{protein:one}} g in a home naan, and about {{protein:large}} g in a large restaurant naan.

foods.answer: A home naan brushed with a teaspoon of butter has about {{kcal:one_tsp}} calories. A large restaurant butter naan comes to about {{outLo}} to {{outHi}}, depending on size.
intro: Butter naan is plain naan brushed with melted butter as it comes out of the tandoor. In restaurants and on delivery apps it's the most ordered bread with butter chicken, dal makhani and paneer dishes, and garlic butter naan adds chopped garlic and coriander to the same butter.
The butter is easy to see but it's the smaller part. The naan itself, and especially its size, decides most of the number.

text: A restaurant butter naan is usually two to three times the size of a home naan, and the butter is spread over all of it. Some places add a second brush of butter before serving, and garlic butter naan often has more.
No lab has measured a restaurant butter naan, so the range below scales this naan and its teaspoon of butter up 2 to 3 times, in line with USDA's 177 g, 10-inch naan.

changes: Each teaspoon of butter adds about 35 calories, and a teaspoon of ghee about 45.
Naan size counts for more than the butter. A large naan is about three times a home one before any butter goes on.
Garlic butter naan uses the same butter, plus garlic and coriander that add very little.
Sharing one large naan between two is about half of the outside range each.
method: The naan is the one in The Art & Science of Cooking, a standard Indian cookery textbook (via the Indian Nutrient Databank), with 80 g of maida for 2 naans. The textbook brushes 2 naans with a teaspoon of butter, which is the half-teaspoon row in the table. Butter values are from USDA, the rest from IFCT 2017.
Restaurant sizes follow USDA's survey data, where a 10-inch naan weighs 177 g.

faq.q: How many calories are in 1 butter naan?
faq.a: About {{kcal:one_tsp}} for a home naan with a teaspoon of butter. A large restaurant butter naan is about {{kcal:large}}.

faq.q: How many calories are in 2 butter naans?
faq.a: Two home butter naans with a teaspoon of butter each come to about 420. Two large restaurant ones can pass 1,000.

faq.q: How much more is butter naan than plain naan?
faq.a: About 35 calories for each teaspoon of butter. A home [naan](/calories/naan/) is about {{kcal@naan:one}} plain and about {{kcal:one_tsp}} with a teaspoon of butter.

faq.q: How much protein is in a butter naan?
faq.a: About {{protein:one_tsp}} g in a home butter naan, and about {{protein:large}} g in a large restaurant one. Butter adds almost none.

No analysed value for butter naan was found, so there is no independent cross-check beyond the plain naan page's USDA checks.

foods.answer: One plain dosa (about 33 g of rice and urad dal, cooked with ¾ teaspoon of oil) has about {{kcal:one}} calories, or about {{kcal:dry}} on a non-stick tawa with no oil.
intro: A plain dosa is a fermented batter of rice and urad dal, spread thin on a hot tawa and cooked with a little oil, ghee or butter until crisp. It's eaten across south India for breakfast and dinner, with sambar and coconut chutney, and paper dosa is the same batter spread larger and thinner.
The batter is mostly rice. Without any fat a dosa is about {{kcal:dry}} calories; the oil or ghee on the tawa is what moves it from there.
foods.portionsCaption: Batter as below. Oil, ghee or butter on the tawa is counted per dosa. Sambar and chutney are not included.

outside.basis: USDA FNDDS lists dosas at 35 g (small), 80 g (medium) and 155 g (large); 155 / 80 = 1.9, used as the top size. Butter up to a teaspoon is a stated assumption.
text: Restaurant plain dosas and paper dosas are often much bigger than home ones, and many places finish them with butter or ghee. USDA's survey data lists dosas from 35 g for a small one to 155 g for a large one.
The range below runs from a dosa like this one up to one about 1.9 times the size, with up to a teaspoon of butter on top.

changes: Fat on the tawa is the biggest variable. Each teaspoon of oil adds about 40 calories, and a teaspoon of ghee about 45.
A bigger or thicker dosa uses more batter. Paper dosa is thin but large, so it often has more than a home dosa.
Sambar and chutney are separate dishes. ICMR-NIN counts a cup of sambar at about 110 calories and 2 tablespoons of coconut chutney at about 120.
Rava dosa, neer dosa and pesarattu use different batters and have their own values. Masala dosa adds a potato filling: see [masala dosa](/calories/masala-dosa/).
method: The recipe is the plain dosa in Basic Food Preparation, a standard Indian cookery manual (via the Indian Nutrient Databank): 50 g raw rice, 50 g parboiled rice, 30 g urad dal and a little fenugreek, making 4 dosas, cooked with 1 tablespoon of oil or butter between them. That's about ¾ teaspoon (3.4 g) per dosa. Values are from IFCT 2017.
Fermenting and cooking change the water in the batter, not the calories, so each dosa is counted as a quarter of the batter plus the fat on the tawa.

range.text: Published figures for one dosa differ because dosas differ in size. ICMR-NIN counts a dosa at 125 calories, and USDA's survey data puts a medium 80 g dosa at about 170. A home plain dosa usually lands between {{kcal:dry}} and 170, depending on size and oil.
range.reason: USDA FNDDS medium dosa (80 g, 168 kcal) is 17% above this page's textbook dosa; NIN's 125 is 13% below. Size differs. Shown as a range.

faq.q: How many calories are in 1 plain dosa?
faq.a: About {{kcal:one}} for a home dosa cooked with ¾ teaspoon of oil, and about {{kcal:dry}} without oil. A large restaurant dosa can be close to twice that.

faq.q: How many calories are in a dosa with ghee?
faq.a: About {{kcal:ghee}} with a teaspoon of ghee on the tawa.

faq.q: How many calories are in dosa with sambar and chutney?
faq.a: Add them separately. ICMR-NIN counts a cup of sambar at about 110 calories and 2 tablespoons of coconut chutney at about 120, so a dosa with both is about 375 to 400.

faq.q: Which has fewer calories, dosa or idli?
faq.a: Per piece, an [idli](/calories/idli/) at about {{kcal@idli:medium}} calories, because a dosa uses more batter and is cooked with oil. Two idlis are about {{kcal@idli:two}}, a little less than one dosa.

faq.q: How much protein is in a plain dosa?
faq.a: About {{protein:one}} g, from the rice and urad dal. Sambar adds a few grams more.

intro: Uttapam is made from the same kind of rice and urad dal batter as dosa, but it's poured thick, topped with onion, tomato, chilli and coriander, and cooked slowly on both sides with oil. It's a breakfast and tiffin dish across Tamil Nadu and Karnataka, and a standard on Udupi restaurant menus.
Because it's thick, one uttapam holds more batter than a home dosa. The toppings add little; the batter and the oil on the tawa make up most of the number.
foods.portionsCaption: Made as below, with the tawa oil counted in. Sambar and chutney are not included.

text: Restaurant uttapams are often thicker and wider than home ones, and some places finish them with butter or serve a ghee version. The toppings are similar.
We found no lab measurement of restaurant uttapam, so the range below assumes one up to 1.5 times this size, with up to a teaspoon of butter.

changes: Thickness and size matter most. A thick uttapam can hold twice the batter of a home dosa.
Each teaspoon of oil on the tawa adds about 40 calories. Uttapam is cooked on both sides, so it usually takes more oil than a dosa.
The onion and tomato topping adds under 20 calories an uttapam.
Cheese or paneer uttapam adds more: a 20 g grating of cheese is about 60 calories.
Rava uttapam uses semolina and curd instead of rice and dal, and has its own values.
method: The recipe is the onion tomato uttapam in The Art & Science of Cooking, a standard Indian cookery textbook (via the Indian Nutrient Databank): 60 g rice, 20 g urad dal, 50 g each of onion and tomato and green chilli, cooked with 3 teaspoons of oil, making 2 uttapams. Values are from IFCT 2017.
The databank also lists a cup of oil 'for frying', which would make each uttapam over 600 calories. Uttapam is cooked on a tawa, so only the 3 teaspoons are counted here.

range.text: Basic Food Preparation, another standard manual, makes a smaller mixed-vegetable uttapam at about 175 calories. Uttapams vary in size and oil, so most come to between about 175 and {{kcal:one}}.
range.reason: INDB's per-uttapam value for Basic Food Preparation's uttapam (BFP152, 174 kcal) is 19% below this page's ASC148 uttapam. That uttapam uses about 33 g of grain each against 40 g here. Shown as a range.

faq.q: How many calories are in 1 uttapam?
faq.a: About {{kcal:one}} for an onion tomato uttapam made at home with 1½ teaspoons of oil. A mini uttapam is about {{kcal:mini}}.

faq.q: Which has more calories, uttapam or dosa?
faq.a: Usually the uttapam, because it's thicker and holds more batter and oil. A home [plain dosa](/calories/plain-dosa/) is about {{kcal@plain-dosa:one}} calories against about {{kcal:one}} for an uttapam.

faq.q: How much protein is in an uttapam?
faq.a: About {{protein:one}} g, from the rice and urad dal.

faq.q: Is uttapam batter the same as dosa batter?
faq.a: Very close. Many homes use leftover dosa batter for uttapam, often after it's turned a little sour. The calories per gram of batter are about the same.
